summary: God renews a covenant with Abram, renames him Abraham, promises many nations and Canaan, and requires circumcision of every male in his household, including purchased servants and infants. Sarai is renamed Sarah and promised a son, Isaac; Abraham laughs and asks about Ishmael, who receives a separate blessing, and Abraham circumcises the household that day.
whyItMatters: This chapter specifies both the promised family line through Sarah and the covenant sign imposed on the whole male household. Its inclusion of infants and purchased men makes the power and bodily stakes of the command visible.

context.author: Genesis names no historical writer. Jewish and Christian tradition associates the Torah with Moses; the book briefing describes older traditions shaped into a final literary form, without a settled account of every stage.
context.audience: The book addresses Israel through a story of shared human origins and the family from whom Israel traces its ancestry; no single first audience is named in this chapter.
context.date: The narrated events belong to primeval or ancestral time, not to a securely dated writing event. Major stages of Genesis are often placed across the monarchic to Persian periods, with exact models and dates debated.
context.setting: Abraham’s household when he is ninety-nine years old, with the promised land named as Canaan.
context.literaryForm: Extended divine covenant speech with name changes, bodily sign, competing hopes for sons, and obedience report.

before.text: Hagar has borne Ishmael to Abram after Sarai’s failed attempt to obtain a child through her servant. The covenant speech now specifies Sarah’s own promised son.

here.text: Distinguish the broad promises to Abraham, the circumcision requirement for the household, and the different statements about Isaac and Ishmael.

after.text: Visitors come to Abraham, repeat that Sarah will have a son, and the narrative turns toward Sodom and Abraham’s appeal for justice.

outline.heading: Covenant and Abraham’s new name
outline.note: God promises nations, kings, descendants, and Canaan.

outline.heading: Circumcision for the male household
outline.note: The bodily covenant sign includes infants and purchased men, with a cutoff warning.

outline.heading: Sarah named and promised a son
outline.note: God blesses Sarah and Abraham laughs at the prospect of their child.

outline.heading: Isaac and Ishmael distinguished
outline.note: Abraham pleads for Ishmael; God blesses him while naming Isaac as covenant successor.

outline.heading: Household circumcised
outline.note: Abraham, Ishmael, and all males in the household receive the sign that day.

keyVerses.text: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your offspring after you.
keyVerses.why: The covenant is explicitly extended across generations.

keyVerses.text: He who is eight days old shall be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he who is born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your offspring.
keyVerses.why: The sign reaches infants and males acquired from outside the family.

keyVerses.text: As for Ishmael, I have heard you. Behold, I have blessed him, and will make him fruitful, and will multiply him exceedingly. He will become the father of twelve princes, and I will make him a great nation.
keyVerses.why: Ishmael receives a blessing even though the covenant line is specified through Isaac.

questions.question: Why does Abram become Abraham?
questions.answer: God connects the new name with becoming father of a multitude of nations. The change is part of the covenant speech, alongside promises of offspring, kings, and land.

questions.question: Does Sarah receive a promise of her own child?
questions.answer: Yes. God renames her Sarah, says she will bear a son, and later names him Isaac. Abraham’s laughter and question about age show how surprising this is after years without her child.

questions.question: Who must undergo circumcision under this command?
questions.answer: Every male in the household is included, among them eight-day-old infants, those born in the house, and men bought from foreigners. The passage presents it as a covenant requirement and does not discuss the consent of infants or purchased servants.

questions.question: Is Ishmael ignored when Isaac is promised?
questions.answer: No. Abraham asks for Ishmael, and God says he has heard, blesses him, and promises a great nation from him. The text then distinguishes that blessing from the covenant it says will be established with Isaac.

questions.question: What does being “cut off” mean here?
questions.answer: The speech warns that an uncircumcised male will be cut off from his people for breaking the covenant. The warning is severe, but the chapter gives no enforcement process or fuller definition of the penalty.

questions.question: What is the “token” of the covenant?
questions.answer: God calls circumcision of the foreskin the bodily token of the agreement with Abraham and his offspring. The sign is repeated in the obedience scene when all males of the household are circumcised.

questions.question: Does the land promise tell readers how to treat current inhabitants?
questions.answer: The promise names Canaan as an everlasting possession while calling it a land where Abraham is traveling. This chapter gives no procedure for relations with its inhabitants or authorization for modern displacement.

questions.question: How quickly does Abraham act after the speech?
questions.answer: He circumcises Ishmael and all males born or bought in his house on the same day. The narrative gives their ages, highlighting that both father and son and the wider dependent household are involved.

glossary.def: The removal of the foreskin required here as the male household’s covenant sign.
A visible sign of the covenant; here the term refers to circumcision.
The son promised to Sarah and Abraham, explicitly named as the future covenant successor.
